evidence.claim: Recomputed from the CSV: the rows sum to 148+121+66+71+48+39+47 = 540, which matches the stated total. Actionable pages sum to 0+2+0+63+41+37+30 = 173, so the actionable rate is 173/540, about 32.0%. evidence.limitations: This is arithmetic on aggregated counts. It assumes 'led_to_human_action' is recorded reliably and that demoted alerts would not hide real incidents (queue-lag-warning did have 2 actions). Per-day figures assume pages are spread evenly over 90 days.

evidence.claim: DST dates in 2026: the US springs forward Sunday 8 March 2026 and falls back Sunday 1 November 2026. The EU moves to summer time on 29 March 2026 and back on 25 October 2026 (last Sundays of March and October, at 01:00 UTC). The US-Europe offset is therefore 1 hour shorter from 8-29 March and from 25 October to 1 November.

source.title: Daylight Saving Time 2026: When Clocks Change in Every Major Country

evidence.applicability: Refutes the planner assumption of a constant 9-hour offset. PT-Berlin is 9h normally and 8h for about 3 weeks in March and 1 week in late Oct/early Nov (G3, C5).

evidence.claim: Shift-boundary analysis, derived from the offsets in E10. With a 9h offset, Berlin 07:00-19:00 CET corresponds to 22:00-10:00 PT, so SF covers 10:00-22:00 PT. Neither office then has duty in the local 22:00-06:00 window, nor in the German statutory night window of 23:00-06:00. The alternative, Berlin 05:00-17:00 CET (20:00-08:00 PT) with SF on 08:00-20:00 PT, puts Berlin 1 hour (05:00-06:00) inside the German night window. During the 8h-offset weeks, if boundaries are fixed to Berlin local time (07:00-19:00), SF's half becomes 11:00-23:00 PT, adding 1 hour of SF local late evening (22:00-23:00). If boundaries are fixed to SF time instead, Berlin's shift shifts to 06:00-18:00.
evidence.applicability: G3: a 07:00-19:00 Berlin / 10:00-22:00 PT split removes local-night duty for both offices, which is central to C1 and C4. Overnight call-outs for Berlin, and the 11h-rest effects that come with them, would be largely avoided, though a call-out ending at 19:00 still pushes next-day start to 06:00 or later.
evidence.limitations: This is my own reasoning. Weekends, holidays and incidents that cross the boundary are not modelled here (see E20-E26 for the ArbZG s.3 and s.9-11 constraints). Whether actionable pages cluster near boundaries is unknown because there are no timestamps (E3).

evidence.claim: Per-person burden, derived from the roster and CSV. Option (a): each engineer is primary 1 week in 9, and with a secondary also on a 9-person rotation, is on call (primary or secondary) about 2 weeks in 9. The 24/7 night exposure is unchanged. Option (b): each office covers 84 h/week, which is about 16.8 h per SF engineer per week vs 21 h per Berlin engineer per week, so Berlin carries about 25% more on-call hours per person (or, in weekly blocks, 1 week in 5 for SF vs 1 week in 4 for Berlin). Raw load is 540 pages/90 days, about 6/day, about 42 per 24/7 week (about 3 per 12h shift). After removing the 3 noise alerts it is about 2.3/day, about 16 per week (about 1.1 per 12h shift).

evidence.limitations: Pages per shift assume an even split. The 58% night figure (unverified) would shift more pages into the Berlin half under a 22:00-10:00 PT split. How the secondary would be paged, and how often, is unknown.

evidence.claim: German secondary sources on ArbZG s.5: employees must have at least 11 hours of uninterrupted rest after daily working time ends. On-call standby (Rufbereitschaft) counts as rest unless the employee is actually called to work. A call-out generally restarts the full 11-hour rest regardless of how long it lasted. There are exceptions (e.g. hospitals, s.5(3)) and room for collective-agreement deviations.
evidence.applicability: Consistent with HR note E5. Under option (a), any Berlin primary or secondary with night call-outs triggers the rest restart and reduces next-day capacity (C4, G5).
evidence.limitations: The statute text was not retrieved (the fetch of gesetze-im-internet.de failed). Search snippets only. Exact attribution of each point to each domain is approximate.

verification.method: WebFetch of gesetze-im-internet.de failed (ENOTFOUND); search snippets only

evidence.claim: Some German commentary (a Luther law-firm publication from 2012, an LMU ZAAR lecture handout, hrworks) argues that trivial interruptions such as a short phone call or email may not count as interrupting the rest period ('Bagatelle' / teleological reduction). The boundary is disputed and fluid.
evidence.applicability: Even a short remote acknowledgement of a page at night may restart rest under the strict view. This is a legal uncertainty that favours keeping Berlin off night duty, and it should go to labour counsel (G5, C4).
evidence.limitations: A minority or contested view, from search snippets only. Not case law.

evidence.claim: Under BetrVG s.87(1) no.2 the works council has co-determination rights over the start and end of daily working time and how it is distributed. On-call (Rufbereitschaft) periods count as working time for this purpose, so both introducing on-call and drawing up the on-call plan need works council agreement. The local works council is normally competent. If no agreement is reached, the conciliation board (Einigungsstelle) decides and its ruling replaces the agreement (s.87(2)). Whether s.87(1) no.3 applies is disputed; most sources say it usually does not for permanent on-call arrangements.

source.title: IG Metall Muster BV Notdienst und Rufbereitschaft

evidence.applicability: Confirms that the HR note's approval gate is a legal requirement for both options (a secondary role and a 12h shift plan both change the Berlin on-call plan). Deadlock leads to the Einigungsstelle, which could take longer than 4-8 weeks (C4, C6).
evidence.limitations: Search snippets of secondary sources. The statute text could not be fetched. Whether alert-tuning changes alone need works council involvement was not researched (note that monitoring-related co-determination under s.87(1) no.6 was not checked).

evidence.claim: German on-call pay varies by agreement. In public-sector tariffs (TVöD), on-call under 12h is paid hourly at 12.5% of the hourly wage on weekdays (15% Saturday, 25% Sunday/holiday), and periods over 12h at a flat daily rate. In the private sector there is no statutory rate; pay is set by contract or works agreement, often 12.5-25% of the hourly wage. Actual call-out work is paid as working time.
evidence.applicability: For G5 pay fairness: the company's actual 'collective policy' allowance is unknown, so it cannot be compared with the US $400/week. A 12h daytime shift may pay differently from a 24h block depending on the agreement.
evidence.limitations: These are general examples, not the company's policy. Some figures come from blogs or older tariff versions. Search snippets only.

evidence.claim: ArbZG s.9 sets a general ban on employing workers on Sundays and public holidays, and s.10 lists statutory exceptions. A KomNet (NRW labour-protection advisory service) answer classes an IT company under s.10(1) no.14 (maintaining data networks and computer systems). Any Sunday or holiday work under the s.10 exceptions requires that the work cannot be done on working days. A further KomNet answer on repair work under no.14 says such work does not have to be notified to the authority, but the working hours must be recorded (s.16(2) ArbZG).
evidence.applicability: D1 / C4: weekend and holiday call-outs by Berlin engineers on a 07:00-19:00 shift are banned under s.9 by default. They would most likely be permitted under s.10(1) no.14 for incident response on production systems, because a live outage cannot wait until a working day. This exception covers responding to genuinely urgent alerts. It does not obviously cover routine or deferrable weekend work, which is another reason to demote noise alerts (E2) so that weekend call-outs are limited to non-deferrable incidents. Call-out hours on Sundays and holidays must be recorded.
evidence.limitations: Single search-result synthesis. The exact statutory wording of s.10(1) no.14 was not retrieved (the search summary said it did not find it). The fetches of gesetze-im-internet.de and lxgesetze.de failed with ENOTFOUND. KomNet answers are advisory opinions, not binding rulings or case law. Which point comes from which listed URL is approximate. CORROBORATED is not claimed because the corroborating refs were not individually inspected.

verification.method: WebSearch result summary only; WebFetch of lxgesetze.de/arbzg/10 and gesetze-im-internet.de/arbzg/__3.html failed (ENOTFOUND)

evidence.claim: Rufbereitschaft counts as rest time as long as the employee is not called on to work. Time actually spent working during Rufbereitschaft (the call-out) counts as working time.
evidence.applicability: D1 / C4: a 12-hour 07:00-19:00 Rufbereitschaft shift is not 12 hours of working time under ArbZG. Only call-out time counts toward the s.3 daily maximum, together with any regular work done that day. The 12h on-call window therefore does not breach s.3 by itself. The risk comes from weekday call-outs on top of a normal 8h workday (see E23).
evidence.limitations: The rest-time/working-time distinction appears in this run's search summary and in the earlier-run snippets cited for E13 (different domains), so CORROBORATED rests on snippets, not on inspected pages. Statute and BAG/CJEU case law were not retrieved.

verification.method: Search snippets from two independent search calls/domains

evidence.claim: If an activity does not fall under the s.10 exceptions, Sunday or holiday employment can be authorised by the competent authority under ArbZG s.13 (e.g. s.13(3) no.2 on application). A Saxon administrative-court case on telephone service support dealt with such an s.13 authorisation.
evidence.applicability: Fallback route for D1 if counsel concludes that weekend/holiday platform on-call call-outs fall outside s.10(1) no.14. Authorisation would add lead time to the rollout (C6).
evidence.limitations: Single search-result summary. The decision was not read. The facts (call-centre service support) differ from platform incident response.

evidence.claim: ArbZG s.3 (content not retrieved in this run; from general background knowledge only): daily working time on working days (Werktage, Mon-Sat) may not exceed 8 hours. It may be extended to up to 10 hours if it averages 8 hours over 6 calendar months or 24 weeks. Applied to the Berlin 07:00-19:00 design, the 12h standby is not working time (E21). But if a Berlin engineer works a normal 8h day while on shift and has call-outs on top, more than 2h of call-out time would push the day past the 10h ceiling. Any time over 8h must also be offset within the averaging period.
evidence.applicability: D1 / C4: this suggests (unverified) that on-call weekdays need reduced regular hours, or a rule that call-out time replaces regular work, plus working-time recording that covers call-outs. With noise removed (about 1.1 pages per 12h shift, E12) the ceiling is less likely to be hit, but long incidents could still breach it.
evidence.limitations: The statute text could not be retrieved (gesetze-im-internet.de and lxgesetze.de unreachable; search budget exhausted before a s.3 search ran). The 8h/10h/6-month/24-week figures come from the request framing and model background knowledge. Must be confirmed by labour counsel.

verification.method: Not retrieved; s.3 search blocked by exhausted WebSearch budget

evidence.claim: ArbZG s.11 (not retrieved; background knowledge only): even where Sunday work is permitted, at least 15 Sundays per year must stay work-free. Employees who work on a Sunday must get a substitute rest day within 2 weeks (within 8 weeks for a weekday public holiday). Sunday and holiday working time is subject to the s.3 limits. Applied to option (b), a rotation of 4 Berlin engineers covering every weekend would need tracking of which Sundays count as 'worked' for each person.
evidence.applicability: D1 / C3 / C4: affects fairness and capacity for Berlin weekend coverage (each Berlin engineer is on 1 week in 4 under weekly blocks, so about 13 weekends per year). Whether a Sunday with only standby and no call-out counts as a 'worked' Sunday is unclear: under E21 logic, standby alone may not be employment, but this is unverified.
evidence.limitations: Not retrieved in this run. Whether pure Rufbereitschaft on a Sunday, with no call-out, is itself 'Beschäftigung' under s.9/s.11 was not researched. Needs counsel confirmation.

evidence.claim: Collective-agreement deviations under ArbZG s.7 (daily maximum, rest periods, including extensions beyond 10h where working time regularly includes standby, and adjustment of rest periods for Rufbereitschaft) and s.12 (number of work-free Sundays, substitute rest days) may allow a collective agreement, or a works agreement based on one, to depart from the s.3, s.5 and s.11 defaults. Whether the Berlin entity is covered by any such collective agreement is unknown.
evidence.applicability: D1 / C4 / C6: if the 'collective policy' in HR notes (E5) is an actual collective agreement with s.7/s.12 opening clauses, some constraints in E23-E24 may be relaxed.
